---

What did he do but lie beneath a pear tree, wrapped in a great cloak, meditating upon the heavenly bodies? *Venerable*, whispered the good people of Baltimore, shocked and not a little afraid. Surely, they said, he had taken to strong drink—why else would he keep vigil beneath the stars all night, and why had he never married? But who, indeed, would have him! Neither Ethiopian nor Englishman, neither fortunate nor mad, a capacious bird humming as he composed in his mind yet another impassioned letter to President Jefferson—he could already imagine the reply, courteous and rhetorical. Those who had journeyed to Philadelphia spoke of the statue of Benjamin Franklin before the library, cast in his very likeness and stature. A wife? No, thank you. At dawn he milked the cows, then went inside to set a pot to stew while he slept. The clock he had whittled as a boy still kept time. Neighbors roused him with warm bread and quilts. At nightfall he took up his rifle—a white-maned figure haunting the darkened breast of the Union—and fired at the stars; by chance, one went out. Had he killed it?

*I assure thee, my dear Sir!* Lowering his gaze to fields sweet with the rot of spring, he beheld a government's domed city rising from the morass, spreading outward in a spiral of lights....
outputs.L2: Beyond stretching out beneath a pear tree, swathed in an enormous cloak while contemplating the stars, what activities occupied him? *A man of dignity*, murmured Baltimore's citizens—their tone tinged with unease and suspicion. Rumor held that he'd developed a fondness for hard liquor. What other explanation existed for his nightly vigils beneath the sky, or his bachelorhood? Yet who would choose him as a husband anyway! He belonged fully to neither the Ethiopian nor English world, was neither blessed nor unhinged—a large bird-like figure, humming to himself as he composed, in his imagination, another passionate letter to President Jefferson, already anticipating a courteous, diplomatically-worded response. Travelers returning from Philadelphia claimed the statue of Benjamin Franklin outside the library matched his own stature and appearance precisely. Marriage? He wanted none of it. Each morning at first light, he tended the cows before returning indoors to set a stew simmering as he slept. The timepiece he'd carved during boyhood continued ticking faithfully. His neighbors roused him with fresh loaves and blankets. Come evening, he retrieved his rifle—resembling some silver-haired sentinel patrolling the shadowed expanse of the nation—and fired toward the heavens; remarkably, a star vanished from sight. Had his shot found its mark? *I give you my word, good Sir!* Casting his gaze downward toward fields fragrant with springtime decay, he envisioned a capital city crowned with domes emerging from the swampland, its lights unfurling outward in ever-widening circles....

# The Watcher of the Stars

In the taverns and parlors of Baltimore, tongues wagged about the strange man who lived alone at the edge of town. The community viewed him with a mixture of suspicion and fear, for what respectable soul spent his nights beneath the open sky, gazing at stars instead of gazing into the eyes of a wife? Surely, they whispered over their ale and needlework, he must be some venerable eccentric—perhaps even secretly nursing a bottle in the darkness, for what else could explain a grown man's fascination with the heavens? The absence of a household, of children's voices, of the ordinary rhythms of domestic life, unsettled his neighbors more than any crime could have. They needed an explanation, and drink was easier to imagine than genius.

He existed in a peculiar, unclassifiable space between worlds—not quite Ethiopian in the way the townspeople understood such origins, not quite English in his bearing and learning, belonging fully to neither category they had prepared for him. He was neither the town's fool nor its fortunate son, neither blessed by luck nor afflicted by madness, but something the community lacked the vocabulary to name. In the privacy of his thoughts, he composed elaborate, impassioned letters to President Jefferson—arguments about reason, equality, and the promise of the new nation—and in his imagination, he heard back replies, courteous and rhetorical, the kind of measured diplomatic language that powerful men used to acknowledge without truly answering.

Yet for all the town's gossip and speculation, his days unfolded with a quiet, unadorned simplicity that belied their fantastical theories. He rose before dawn to milk his cows, moving through the mist with the practiced ease of long habit. He cooked his own modest meals, needing no one to tend to him. Time itself he measured by a clock he had carved with his own hands as a boy—a simple wooden mechanism that, against all odds and expectations, still kept faithful time decades later, as if his childhood ingenuity had reached forward to serve the man he'd become.

But when darkness fell, something in him shifted. The ordinary farmer disappeared, and in his place emerged a figure almost mythic in his strangeness—his hair gone white and wild in the moonlight, a rifle in his hands aimed not at any earthly target but at the stars themselves. One night, by pure chance, his shot found its mark, and a star winked out of existence. He stood there afterward in the sudden silence, rifle still smoking, wondering with genuine unease whether he had actually killed something—some celestial creature, some cosmic law—or whether the universe had simply chosen that moment to let one small light go out on its own.

It was in the gentler hours, watching the spring fields stretch toward the horizon, that his private visions grew largest. Standing alone in that green expanse, he imagined the nation's capital rising up from the very earth beneath his feet—not as mere buildings and streets, but as a spiraling city of lights, ascending toward the heavens like some earthly constellation of human ambition. In that vision, his own solitary watching of the stars became inseparable from the larger dream of the republic itself: two acts of faith, both improbable, both born from watching the darkness and daring to imagine what might yet be illuminated.

# The Solitary Astronomer of Baltimore County

In the rolling hills outside Baltimore, where tobacco fields gave way to modest farmland, there lived a man whose habits set him apart from all his neighbors. He was of mixed blood—African and perhaps something else besides, though no one asked directly, and he offered no explanations. His skin marked him as other in a land governed by rigid categories, and his solitary ways only deepened the community's sense that here was someone fundamentally strange, perhaps even touched by something beyond ordinary understanding.

By day, he tended his small farm with the same quiet diligence that characterized everything he did. His hands, weathered by sun and labor, moved through familiar tasks—planting, tending, harvesting—with the unhurried competence of a man who had made peace with solitary work. He had no wife, no children to carry forward his name or his blood. The women of the county had long since stopped speculating about this absence, settling instead into a comfortable narrative: he was peculiar, perhaps incapable of the ordinary attachments that bound other men to family and community. Pity mixed with their suspicion, a strange brew that allowed them to feel superior even as they wondered, in private moments, what exactly kept him so contentedly alone.

But it was at night that the true strangeness began, the behavior that gave the neighboring farms their most persistent gossip. Long after decent folk had banked their fires and retired to sleep, lights would flicker in his modest home, and sometimes he could be seen outside, standing motionless in his yard, head tilted back, eyes fixed on the vast canopy of stars above. What manner of man kept such hours? What business did a farmer have with the night sky, hour after hour, season after season, as if he were reading some celestial text that only he could decipher?

The rumors grew more elaborate with each telling. Someone claimed to have seen him writing letters—not the simple correspondence of a farmer conducting business, but lengthy missives, covered in dense script, sealed with unusual care. And to whom would such a man write? The whispers suggested, with a mixture of disbelief and dark amusement, that he corresponded with President Jefferson himself. The very idea seemed to confirm what the neighbors had long suspected: the poor man's isolation had curdled into delusion. What could a colored farmer possibly have to say to the President of the United States? What could the President possibly want to hear from him?

Yet beneath the surface of their scorn and pity ran an undercurrent of something else—an unacknowledged unease, perhaps even a flicker of recognition that they could not quite suppress. For this man possessed knowledge that exceeded anything in their own limited experience. He understood the movements of celestial bodies with a precision that bordered on the supernatural to minds unfamiliar with mathematics and astronomy. He had taught himself to calculate the positions of stars, to predict eclipses, to understand the vast mechanical clockwork of the heavens through nothing but patient observation, careful reasoning, and an intellect that burned bright despite—or perhaps because of—its isolation.

The truth, invisible to those who mocked him, was this: the letters were real, and so was their extraordinary content. This man, whom his neighbors dismissed as an oddity, possessed genius of a rare and profound order. His nocturnal observations were not the ravings of a lonely mind but the disciplined work of a self-taught astronomer, a mathematician who had mastered complex calculations without benefit of formal education, without the resources and encouragement that would have been automatically extended to a white man of similar ability. His correspondence with Jefferson was not fantasy but fact—a genuine exchange between a farmer-astronomer and the nation's highest office, touching on matters of science, of human capability, of the very questions about race and intelligence that defined and constrained his existence.

And in the grandest irony of all, this marginalized figure—dismissed, pitied, viewed with suspicion by those who shared his soil but not his vision—played a role in one of the young nation's most ambitious undertakings: the conception and planning of its new capital city. While his neighbors slept, while they gossiped about his strange isolation, this solitary man contributed his mathematical and astronomical expertise to the surveying and design of Washington, D.C., helping to lay out the very streets and boundaries that would house the government of a nation that could not fully see him, could not fully acknowledge what he had accomplished, could not reconcile his brilliance with the racial categories that supposedly determined human worth and capability.

The tragedy and triumph exist side by side in this portrait: a man capable of conceiving cosmic order and civic geometry, reduced in his community's eyes to a curious bachelor with peculiar nocturnal habits. His genius flourished not because of his circumstances but in spite of them, in the solitary hours when he could escape the constraints of a society unable to imagine that greatness might wear his face, might carry his blood, might emerge from a small farm on the outskirts of Baltimore rather than from the halls of privilege and formal education. He remained, to his neighbors, an object of gossip and unease—while quietly, methodically, he helped shape the very foundations of the nation's capital, his contribution as invisible to his community as the distant stars he spent his nights observing were, in their way, entirely visible to him alone.

# What the Venerable History of Baltimore Teaches Us

Baltimore stands as one of America's most historically significant port cities, its venerable streets echoing centuries of maritime commerce, cultural transformation, and resilience. What makes this Maryland city so compelling isn't just its age, but the layered story embedded in its brick rowhouses, harbor views, and diverse neighborhoods.

Founded in 1729, Baltimore quickly grew into a vital shipping hub, its harbor bustling with vessels carrying goods to and from ports around the world. What distinguished Baltimore from other colonial settlements was its strategic position—close enough to the Chesapeake Bay to facilitate trade, yet sheltered enough to provide safe harbor during storms and conflicts.

The venerable Fort McHenry, perhaps the city's most iconic landmark, witnessed the very battle that inspired Francis Scott Key to write what would become the national anthem. Standing before those weathered walls today, visitors often wonder what it must have felt like to witness the rockets' red glare during that pivotal 1814 battle.

What truly defines Baltimore's character, however, extends beyond famous battles and monuments. The city's venerable rowhouse architecture, with their distinctive marble steps and formstone facades, tells stories of immigrant communities who built lives here—German, Irish, Italian, and African American residents who each left indelible marks on the city's culture, cuisine, and traditions.

Baltimore's venerable institutions, from Johns Hopkins University to the Peabody Institute, established the city as a center of learning and innovation. What began as practical necessities—medical advances, musical education—became sources of pride that continue attracting scholars and artists today.

Walking through Fells Point or Federal Hill, one encounters what feels like living history: cobblestone streets that have witnessed centuries of foot traffic, taverns where sailors once gathered, and churches whose bells have rung through generations of triumph and hardship.

Baltimore reminds us that venerable doesn't mean static. This is a city that has continuously reinvented itself while honoring its past—transforming industrial waterfronts into vibrant cultural districts, preserving historic architecture while embracing modern innovation. What Baltimore ultimately teaches us is that true heritage isn't about freezing time, but about carrying forward the lessons and character of what came before into an ever-evolving present.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical, historical-fiction short piece imagining the private life and inner thoughts of Benjamin Banneker, the Black astronomer and almanac maker, as townspeople gossip about his solitary habits.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Watcher of Ellicott's Mills

The gossips say he sleeps by day and wakes by starlight, that he talks to no wife, keeps no proper company, that something in him bends toward strangeness. They watch him from behind curtains as he walks his fields at dusk, an old man now, gray-headed, moving slow beneath the weight of instruments they cannot name.

Let them talk.

He has given his life to a clock he built himself, gear by gear, at twenty-two years old, having seen but one timepiece in all his years—a pocket watch, borrowed, studied, then returned. He took its workings apart in his mind the way other men took apart Scripture, searching for the logic underneath. He carved the wheels from wood. He made time visible, audible, a thing with a voice that struck the hours across his silent farm. This, they might understand, if they asked. They do not ask.

At night he lies in the grass behind his cabin, mathematics tables scattered like fallen leaves around him, and watches the wheeling dark. Jupiter's moons. The creep of Saturn's ring, tilting through its long slow seasons. He has taught himself the language the sky speaks—a grammar of ellipses and returns, of eclipses predicted years in advance and proven true to the minute. When the almanac sells, when Jefferson himself receives his letter and his numbers, Banneker feels something that is not quite triumph. It is closer to relief. *You see? You see I am a man of reason, the same as any man.*

But mostly he does not think of proving anything. Mostly there is only this: the cold ground beneath him, the vast wheel of stars turning with a patience that makes human gossip seem a small, brief noise. He was born free in a country that does not know what to do with that fact. He has no wife because he chose the sky instead, and the sky has never once asked him to sit at the back of any room, or called him three-fifths of what he is.

They see solitude. He calls it study.

They see an old man muttering calculations to himself in a garden gone to seed. He is calculating the moment Venus will cross the face of the sun, a transit that will not come again in his lifetime, and he wants—he *needs*—to be awake for it, to witness what so few will ever see, to hold in his one brief human life a fragment of eternity's clockwork.

Let them gossip in the tavern. Let them wonder at the strange, still man who keeps no company but bees and books and the turning dark. He has conversation enough. Copernicus speaks to him in careful theorems. The old astronomers whisper down through centuries of careful watching. And God, if He is there at all, speaks plainest of all in the metronome-tick of the transiting stars, in the way the world keeps its appointments without fail, without prejudice, without ever once asking a man the color of his hand before allowing him to lift it toward the light.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poetic prose vignette about a self-taught Black scientist in early America who studies the stars at night, is misunderstood by his neighbors, and corresponds with Thomas Jefferson.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Almanac Maker**

Before the frost breaks and the tobacco fields go quiet with sleep, he climbs the ladder to his roof with instruments he ground himself—lenses coaxed from glass and patience, a clock he built to keep the hours honest. Benjamin. Free-born, which the world still finds a thing to remark upon, as if freedom were a costume that might slip.

The neighbors watch him from their windows, this dark man alone with the sky, and they do not know what to call what he does. Some say witchcraft. Some say foolishness—a farmer's son with no schooling worth the name, squinting at Jupiter's moons as if the heavens owed him an accounting. They see a Black man past sixty, unmarried, tending his bees and his garden by day, and by night doing this strange, silent arithmetic with the stars. They cannot fit him into any story they know.

But the sky does not ask what a man's skin is before it shows him Saturn's rings, before it lets him predict, to the minute, when the moon will swallow the sun whole. He works by candlelight after, transcribing what he's witnessed into columns of numbers, into an almanac that farmers three counties over will use to know when to plant. His hands—which have known the plow, which have known his father's freedom papers memorized like scripture—now know the weight of a pen forming letters to the Secretary of State.

*Sir,* he writes, and does not grovel, though the times might expect it. He speaks of Equality. He speaks of the mind's dark and the mind's light, and how the first is not the province of any one people, and the second is not the exclusive gift of any other. He encloses his almanac like evidence, like a psalm.

Jefferson writes back—cautious, polite, a man measuring his words against the scale of his own conscience, which he keeps, like Benjamin's instruments, carefully calibrated, and carefully limited.

Still, the letters exist. Still, the almanacs are printed, sold, used by hands that never think to wonder about the mind that charted them. Still, some autumn nights, an old man climbs to his roof alone, and the same stars that shone on pharaohs, on captains of slave ships, on the whole terrible parade of human history, shine also on him—impartial, immense, and his.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a piece of literary flash fiction blending myth and history, centered on a stargazing free Black man in Maryland who dreams of Washington, D.C.'s creation while enduring rumors and isolation.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Surveyor's Almanac

Benjamin kept his instruments wrapped in oilcloth, the way his grandmother had wrapped her bones against the damp. Brass and glass, patient as scripture. The neighbors said he spoke with spirits when he climbed to his roof at midnight, that a Black man had no business knowing the names of stars, that such knowledge belonged to God alone and perhaps to white men who'd stolen fire before.

Let them talk. The sky did not ask permission to hold its logarithms.

He had learned the ephemeris tables from a borrowed book, taught himself to calculate eclipses the way other men learned scripture—by repetition, by faith that the pattern would hold. When the eclipse came in '89, exact to the minute he'd predicted, his neighbors did not apologize. They simply stopped speaking of it, folded their wonder into silence, the way people do when a thing exceeds what they'd allowed themselves to imagine.

In his dreams, the boundary stones marched themselves into a diamond upon the Potomac's marshy shoulders. He dreamed the city before it existed—broad avenues cut through tobacco fields, a Capitol dome rising like a second moon, and himself walking those unbuilt streets as if he'd always belonged there. In the dream, no one asked him for his freedom papers. In the dream, the stars themselves seemed to approve, Polaris fixed and steady as a witness.

He knew the histories they didn't teach: how Thoth had measured the flooding Nile by starlight, how the Dogon had charted Sirius B before European telescopes confirmed its weight, how his own foremothers had read the sky as a map north long before any surveyor's chain touched this ground. Every civilization birthed its stargazers, its mathematicians of the dark. Why should this new nation's capital be built without one who looked like him among its makers?

The commission needed calculations—latitude, longitude, the precise moment when Regulus would cross the meridian so the boundary stones might be set true. Someone would have to stand in the cold night air of Alexandria and watch, unmoving, while lesser men slept. Someone would have to be trusted with the mathematics of a nation's literal foundation.

He wrote the letter three times before sending it. Not pleading. Stating: *I have observed. I have calculated. I am available.*

The isolation was its own instrument, he'd come to understand—necessary, calibrating. Loneliness had taught him to trust his own observations over the crowd's assumptions. The neighbors who whispered "witch" and "conjure man" had never once asked what he saw when he looked up. They assumed the answer was darkness, absence, superstition. They did not imagine precision. They did not imagine a man charting his own coordinates onto the birth certificate of a nation that had not yet decided if he was a citizen or a thing to be counted as three-fifths of one.

But the stars did not care about census categories. Regulus rose the same for him as for any astronomer in Philadelphia or London or Paris. The mathematics did not require permission. This, perhaps, was the secret his grandmother's God-fearing neighbors could not forgive: that a Black man had found a language—numerical, celestial—that white men could not corrupt with their rumors, could not diminish with their doubt. Two plus two remained four whether spoken by master or slave, free man or bound. The sky kept its own accounting, and he had learned to read the ledger.

Later—not yet, but later—they would remember his name beside the word *founding*, would speak of the free Black astronomer who helped fix the boundaries of the nation's capital, who sat with clock and telescope through cold Maryland nights while the republic's architects slept sound in their certainties.

But that was later, was history's slow correction. For now, there was only the roof, the instruments unwrapped like reliquary, and Benjamin measuring the distance between what was and what his calculations insisted must eventually come to be. Above him, invisible from any earthbound argument, the future capital's meridian aligned itself with the only jury he trusted: the patient, indifferent, mathematically exact stars.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental narrative in a dense, archaic style about Benjamin Banneker's nightly rituals, his unmarried status, his rifle, and his imagined letters to a president, ending with a vision of a new capital city.
counterfactuals.output:
# Of the Solitary Astronomer and His Nightly Watches

In the year of our reckoning, upon the loam of Maryland where the Patapsco bends her dark water through stands of chestnut and sycamore, there dwelt a man of colored blood and uncolored mind, one Benjamin Banneker, bachelor unto his final hour, who took no wife nor sired issue, but married instead the turning heavens, and got upon that union children of pure calculation—ephemerides, almanacks, the plotted courses of Jupiter's moons.

He kept, this solitary man, a rifle above the lintel of his cabin door, oiled and ready as a psalm memorized against the dark, for the nights were long and lonesome in that country, and wolves still came down sometimes from the ridges, and men—white men, riding—came sometimes too, and a Black man alone upon his own freehold land learned early the weight of steel kept close as scripture. He did not hunt for sport. He hunted for the preservation of the hours he required: hours of watching, hours of the wool blanket wrapped about his shoulders whilst he lay upon the frost-hard ground beneath the apple trees, his log-cabin roof having been cut through—by his own hand, with his own saw—that he might observe the stars unimpeded by timber and shingle.

Thus did he keep his nightly ritual, this celibate philosopher: at dusk he supped alone on cornmeal and small beer; at the ringing of some private hour known only to his internal clock (for he had built clocks, wooden-geared and faithful, that struck the hours with more constancy than the parish bell), he took up his rifle in the crook of one arm and his instruments in the other, and went out to lie beneath the wheeling dark.

There, alone, unwived, unfathered-of-children, he composed in his mind letters he would never send, or would send and be met with silence, or would send to Mr. Jefferson himself, then Secretary of State, arguing the plain mathematics of the soul: that the stars know no complexion, that the angle of the elliptic cares nothing for the angle of a man's nose or the curl of his hair, that a mind capable of predicting eclipses to the minute might reasonably be supposed capable of self-governance, of liberty, of the vote.

*Sir*, he composed in the theater of his skull, whilst Orion wheeled his belt above the corn-stubble, *I freely and cheerfully acknowledge that I am of the African race, and in that colour which is natural to them of the deepest dye, and it is under a sense of the most profound gratitude to the Supreme Ruler of the Universe, that I now confess to you, that I am not under that state of tyrannical thraldom, and inhuman captivity, to which too many of my brethren are doomed...*

And in this fevered communion between the solitary man and the imagined seat of power, there rose before his mind's eye—as clear as any transit of Venus he had ever calculated—a vision: a city not yet built, laid out in avenues wide as rivers, radiating from a domed seat of law like spokes from the hub of some celestial wheel, its streets numbered and lettered with the same cold clarity he brought to his own tables of the sun's declination. He saw it (for he would help to survey it, this free Black man with his rifle and his celibate nights and his letters composed in loneliness and sent in hope)—he saw the marshy ground of the Potomac's shore transfigured into avenues that would bear, one distant day, the very name of the man to whom his letters went unanswered, or answered only in the cool diplomatic prose of politicians who praised the almanack whilst declining to act upon its argument.

So he lay, old bachelor beneath the frost, rifle cool against his side, watching Jupiter's moons swim their ancient courses, and dreaming forward into a capital not yet risen from its swamp, a city of reason that might, in some future unwitnessed by him, prove worthy of the calculations he had spent his solitary life perfecting.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a short surreal historical narrative merging biography and folklore, depicting a Black astronomer's solitary genius, his community's suspicion, and his symbolic role in shaping America's capital.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Measure of Shadows

They say Benjamin Banneker slept only when the stars slept, which is to say never, which is to say he became a rumor before he became a man.

The neighbors in Ellicott's Mills spoke of him in careful voices—the free Black farmer who read the sky like scripture, who built a clock from wood alone that kept time truer than any brought from England. They said his grandmother had been a dairymaid from Wessex, his grandfather a prince stolen from Guinea, and that in him these two rivers of blood had made something the town had no name for. So they called it strange. They called it dangerous. A colored man who understood Newton, who corresponded with Jefferson as an equal, who dared correct the great men's arithmetic—this was not knowledge, they whispered. This was theft. As if the heavens themselves were property, and he had trespassed.

In the folklore that grew up around him like kudzu, Banneker did not simply calculate the almanac. He *negotiated* with the constellations. Orion owed him a favor. The story goes that when Pierre L'Enfant abandoned the plans for the new capital in a fury and vanished to France with every drawing, taking the young nation's geometry with him into exile, it was Banneker who reconstructed the entire city from memory alone—not his memory, but the memory of the sky, which he'd been reading since boyhood, and which apparently recorded everything, even the plans of vain Frenchmen.

He sat, in this telling, in a canvas tent on the marshy Potomac flats, mosquitoes singing their own vicious astronomy around his head, and he looked up. The stars, arranged just so, were the city. Pennsylvania Avenue was already written in the angle between two winter constellations. The Capitol's dome was rehearsed nightly in the fullness of the moon. He simply transcribed what was already there, in light that had traveled years to reach him, carrying blueprints older than the republic itself.

This did not happen. And yet: the surveying team he assisted did include him, a free Black man, calculating latitude by starlight while enslaved men labored to clear the very swamp he measured—America's capital rising from ground made possible by chains, laid out in part by hands that could never themselves be chained, not entirely, not by law, though the country tried.

This is the folklore's honest cruelty: it makes him magical because his community—both the one that doubted him and the one that would enslave people beside him—could not otherwise hold the contradiction. A Black genius was either impossible or supernatural. There was no room made for merely, devastatingly, human.

Banneker himself wrote to Jefferson plainly, no stars invoked, no magic: *I freely and cheerfully acknowledge that I am of the African race.* He asked, simply, to be believed. He sent his almanac as proof, calculated with his own hands, no divine dictation, no celestial theft. He asked for the ordinary miracle of being taken at his word.

Jefferson wrote back what such men always write back: complicated, hedging, half-admiring, unwilling to let the whole architecture of his belief collapse under one man's careful mathematics.

The city got built. The stars, indifferent, continued their arithmetic without him. But somewhere in the grid of streets, in the diagonal avenues that still confuse tourists today, there is a story insisting that genius is not always granted room to be simply itself—that sometimes it must first become legend, must first become impossible, before it can be allowed to have been merely, completely true.
